# Freecord

> Free, open source group voice, video, text chat and screen sharing that runs
> in a browser with no account. One person creates a room, shares its link, and
> anyone with the link joins as a guest. Audio, video and screen travel
> directly between participants over WebRTC and are end-to-end encrypted, so
> they never pass through a server.

Freecord is a working application, not a demo, and it is MIT licensed. It is
built and maintained by Henrique Brito. Live at
https://freecord.lattoshenrique.workers.dev and developed in the open at
https://github.com/lattoshenrique/freecord.

## What it does

- **Group voice and video calls** in the browser, up to 8 people per room.
- **Screen sharing**, one person at a time, with three quality presets: Sharp
  (for code and text), Balanced, and Smooth (for video and games).
- **Text chat** with Markdown, sealed in the browser and ephemeral — the
  server relays messages it cannot read, and they disappear with the room.
- **Desktop apps** for macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon), Windows and Linux.
- **Interface in five languages**: English, Portuguese, Spanish, Chinese and
  Japanese, auto-detected from the browser.

## What makes it different

- **No account, ever.** No signup, no email, no password. You create a room and
  send the link. The link is the credential.
- **No media server.** Voice, video and screen sharing flow browser-to-browser
  in a peer-to-peer mesh over native WebRTC, encrypted end to end by default
  (DTLS-SRTP). Our server only relays signaling messages and holds room state,
  so it is not technically capable of watching or recording a call. A
  deployment may optionally enable TURN to relay peers that cannot connect
  directly; a TURN relay forwards encrypted bytes it cannot decrypt, making it
  a relay and never a participant. The hosted service at
  freecord.lattoshenrique.workers.dev has no TURN configured today, so every
  call there is direct peer-to-peer or it does not connect at all.
- **Chat the server cannot read, and does not keep.** Messages are sealed in
  the browser with a key that travels only in the room link's fragment — the
  part after `#`, which browsers never send to a server. Ours relays text it
  cannot decrypt and stores none of it: the chat disappears with the room, with
  no transcript, no recording and no analytics on conversations. The limit is
  the room's own: anyone holding the full link holds the key and can read
  along, exactly as they can walk in.
- **No media vendor and no third-party SDK.** The entire signaling protocol
  lives in the repository, and the whole service runs on free-tier
  infrastructure. The single possible exception is optional TURN: a deployment
  that turns it on may point at a managed provider, though TURN is an open
  protocol behind one configuration field, so a self-hosted coturn drops in
  unchanged. Either way the relay forwards encrypted bytes it cannot read,
  which is a categorically smaller exposure than a media vendor. The hosted
  service has no TURN credentials set, so it currently uses none.

## Honest limits

Stated plainly, because they are engineering facts rather than marketing:

- **8 people per room.** This is a real limit of a peer-to-peer mesh, not a
  paywall or a preference: each participant uploads a copy of their stream to
  every other participant, so upload bandwidth becomes the bottleneck past
  roughly eight people with video. Screen video is an exception — it
  propagates through a relay tree with a fanout of 3, so its quality no longer
  degrades as the room fills.
- **Some restrictive networks cannot connect media at all.** Corporate
  networks and symmetric CGNAT often cannot establish a direct peer-to-peer
  path, and reaching them needs a TURN relay. TURN is supported and optional,
  but the hosted service does not have it configured today, so those peers
  fall back to public STUN and fail to connect. Text chat still works for
  them, because it travels over the signaling WebSocket rather than
  peer-to-peer.
- **Chat does not survive a reload.** That is the privacy decision, not an
  oversight.
- **Sealed chat hides the words, not the pattern.** Sender names, timestamps
  and room membership are signaling data, stamped by our server and visible to
  it; only message text is sealed. There is no forward secrecy — one key per
  room for the room's whole life. And because the key rides in the URL,
  sharing a screen with the address bar visible, or pasting a screenshot of
  it, hands the key to everyone who sees it.
- **Rooms are disposable.** A room with nobody in it for 15 minutes ceases to
  exist and its link stops working.

## Privacy

There are no user accounts, so there is no user data. Rooms hold a display name
someone typed and nothing else. Chat text is sealed in the browser and never
written to storage, so the server relays messages it cannot read. Media is
end-to-end encrypted between participants. Room links are unguessable random
slugs (72 bits of entropy), are never indexed, and are excluded from the
sitemap and from crawling.

## Documentation

- [Architecture](https://github.com/lattoshenrique/freecord/blob/main/docs/architecture.md):
  the detailed technical document — the peer-to-peer mesh and its real costs,
  the screen relay tree, how signaling works, how a room expires, the two
  server edges over one shared core, and the deliberate debts of the MVP.
- [README](https://github.com/lattoshenrique/freecord/blob/main/README.md):
  the stack, how to run it locally, and how to deploy it.

## How it is built

React and Vite on the client, with the WebRTC mesh hand-written rather than
taken from an SDK. The server core is transport-independent TypeScript with two
edges over it: a Node/Fastify process for development, and a Cloudflare Worker
with one Durable Object per room, which is what serves production. The desktop
app is an Electron shell around the production page that adds a native screen
picker and system media permissions.
